passages.context: The complete chapter heading and body were inspected at artifact lines 14194–14214. passages.context: The complete chapter body was inspected at artifact lines 17603-17633, under the heading 'That the world and time had both one beginning, and the one did not anticipate the other'. The heading occupies lines 17603-17604 and the body begins at 17606.

passages.context: The complete chapter body was inspected at artifact lines 17636-17677, under the heading 'Of the nature of the first days, which are said to have had morning and evening, before there was a sun'. Augustine holds that the first three days passed without a sun, that light was made by the word of God and separated from the darkness, and that what kind of light it was lies beyond the senses. The remainder of the chapter, at lines 17648-17677, offers the figurative reading of morning and evening as the creature's knowledge and runs through the sixth day. The heading occupies lines 17636-17637.

passages.context: The complete chapter body was inspected at artifact lines 20768-20812, under the heading 'Of that death which can affect an immortal soul, and of that to which the body is subject': the soul called immortal because it does not cease to live and feel, the body called mortal because it can be forsaken of all life; the death of the soul when God forsakes it and the death of the body when the soul forsakes it; the death of the whole man as the compound of the two; the second death that follows; the appeal to Matthew 10:28; and the closing judgment that the first and bodily death is 'to the good it is good, and evil to the evil' while the second can be good for none. The chapter is the tradition's most careful early statement of what the word death is being used to name.

passages.context: The complete chapter body was inspected at artifact lines 21111-21195, under the heading 'Whether one can both be living and dead at the same time': the three times and three corresponding states; the argument that a man is never in death because before death he lives and after it he is dead; the comparison with the unlocatable present instant of time; the question whether it follows that there is no death of the body at all; Augustine's refusal to draw that conclusion; his decision to keep speaking in the customary way on the warrant of scriptural usage, quoting Psalm 6:6; and the closing remark about the damned as endlessly dying. The chapter is the classical statement of the aporia about the moment of death, and Augustine leaves it unresolved.
passages.notes: The chapter heading is at artifact line 21111 and the body begins at 21113. The related chapters are 13.9 (whether the moment of death belongs to the dying or the dead) and 13.10 (life as a race toward death), immediately preceding in the same artifact. passages.context: Complete chapter XVII.8 body, read with its heading at lines 7575-7576 and the following chapter XVII.9 heading at lines 7671-7673. Augustine first narrates Nathan's message to David and quotes 2 Samuel 7:8-16, then explains why the promised everlasting house is fulfilled in Christ rather than exhausted by Solomon. The historical English translation of Book XVII is George Wilson's, as this edition's front matter states; Marcus Dods is the editor. The chapter uses Psalm 72 in Hebrew numbering (canonical Vulgate Psalm 71) and 1 Corinthians 3:17 as supporting parallels, rather than making this one passage a separate commentary fragment on each prooftext.

In the initial quotation, the house-building clause at lines 7599-7600 differs from the Clementine/Douay wording of 2 Samuel 7:11; that source-local difference is preserved. The complete natural biblical unit reaches canonical 2 Kings (= modern 2 Samuel) 7:1-16: the opening explains the proposed house and God's never-commanded cedar house from 7:1-7, before quoting and expounding Nathan's promise at 7:8-16. The whole chapter is transcribed, with no extension to David's prayer at 7:18-29.

passages.context: The complete chapter body was inspected at artifact lines 17748-17782: Augustine's 'amicable controversy' with tender-hearted Christians who held that the damned would be delivered after a fixed term, his report that Origen went further and included the devil and his angels, his statement that the Church condemned Origen for this and for the ceaseless alternation of happiness and misery, and the reductio that a merciful principle consistently applied would have to reach the devil himself.
passages.notes: The chapter heading is at artifact line 17748. Augustine's report of what 'the Church' condemned in Origen is his own summary and is not a citation of a conciliar act; the nearest conciliar-style text registered elsewhere in this library is the 543 Constantinopolitan canon printed by Denzinger at DS 411.
